tldr: By combining geometric admittance control (GAC) for precise task-space feedback with residual reinforcement learning, and introducing a reference frame that eliminates pelvis oscillations, ResGAC achieves millimeter- and degree-level end-effector SE(3) tracking on a real humanoid even during walking and whole-body motion.
overview:
When humanoid robots perform practical tasks, walking naturally is not enough; they must move their hands with millimeter- and degree-level precision while stepping and balancing. However, floating-base oscillations, ground-impact shocks during walking, gravity acting on the arms, and dynamic coupling between the arms and torso make high-precision end-effector pose tracking (SE(3) tracking) exceptionally difficult.

To solve this, the authors propose "ResGAC," a framework that elegantly blends classical control theory with modern reinforcement learning. First, geometric admittance control (GAC) generates nominal arm joint-position targets based on geometric SE(3) task-space errors. Residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL) then operates in the shared joint-position action space to compensate for gravity and unmodeled dynamic discrepancies while coordinating lower-body locomotion and balance. Furthermore, to prevent pelvis oscillations during walking from bleeding into end-effector targets, they introduce a "ground-attached heading frame" that isolates planar translational motion.

In experiments on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, ResGAC significantly outperformed representative baselines like SONIC in standing tracking accuracy, achieving errors around 6 mm in translation and under 2° in rotation. It also demonstrated a 90% success rate in a peg-in-hole task (versus 50% for the baseline) and achieved accurate world-frame positioning in a mime-like task where the end-effector stayed stationary in space while the lower body moved vigorously.
contributions: Proposed ResGAC, integrating geometric admittance control (GAC) with residual reinforcement learning in a shared joint-position action space to achieve both geometric task-space feedback and learned whole-body coordination.

Introduced a ground-attached heading frame leveraging a left-invariant geometric formulation, preserving planar locomotion while isolating pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from manipulation reference targets.

Demonstrated superior accuracy over baselines on a real Unitree G1 compact humanoid across standing tracking, end-effector stabilization during walking, a peg-in-hole task (90% success rate), and world-frame pose tracking during lower-body motion (mime task).

sections.heading: Why is precise humanoid end-effector tracking so difficult?
sections.summary: Humanoid control is shifting from natural whole-body motions to task-space manipulation, but controlling 6-DoF end-effector poses (SE(3)) with millimeter accuracy amid floating-base sway and walking impacts remains a major challenge. This section covers the motivation behind ResGAC's residual approach combining structured model-based control with RL and careful reference frame selection.
sections.details:
In recent years, large-scale imitation learning and reinforcement learning have enabled humanoid robots to acquire remarkably agile and natural whole-body locomotion. However, when performing real-world manipulation—such as grasping objects or handling tools—simply walking is not enough. The robot must track end-effector target poses (6-DoF position and orientation, i.e., $SE(3)$) with extreme accuracy while maintaining balance and stepping.

This is difficult because humanoids lack a fixed base on the ground (they are floating-base systems). Ground impact forces from walking, torso swaying, gravity on the arms, and dynamic coupling all reflect directly onto the hands. While most conventional methods track dense whole-body joint trajectories, real-world tasks are naturally commanded in task space: "move the hand here." Yet tracking task-space goals using pure reinforcement learning often struggles to deliver fine positional and rotational precision.

Another commonly overlooked issue is which reference frame to define the hand target in. If commands are defined relative to the pelvis, periodic pelvis roll, pitch, and heave (vertical motion) from walking directly leak into the end-effector reference, causing unnecessary perturbations.

To tackle these challenges, the authors propose ResGAC. It uses geometric admittance control (GAC) for geometric task-space feedback, while residual RL compensates for unmodeled dynamics and lower-body coordination. By pairing this with a reference frame that strips away unwanted pelvis oscillations, high-precision tracking becomes possible on real humanoids.

sections.heading: Lie groups and whole-body control formulation
sections.summary: This section outlines the Lie group representations, homogeneous transformation matrices, and Jacobians needed to rigorously handle 3D poses. It then formulates the whole-body tracking problem: taking planar velocity and end-effector pose commands and outputting joint-position targets for low-level PD controllers.
sections.details:
### II-A Lie Group and Frame Conventions
Controlling a humanoid's end-effector requires handling both 3D position and rotation without singularities. The paper therefore adopts Lie group notation based on the 3D special orthogonal group $SO(3)$ and special Euclidean group $SE(3)$.
Three primary coordinate frames are defined: the world frame ($W$) with a fixed origin, the manipulation reference frame ($R$) used for targets and controllers, and the end-effector frame ($E$). The reference frame $R$ can be the pelvis frame $P$ or a heading frame described later. The end-effector pose $g_{RE} \in SE(3)$ consists of a rotation matrix $R_{RE}$ and position vector $p_{RE}$, computed in real time via forward kinematics. Relative velocity in the end-effector frame (body twist) and the relative Jacobian $J_{RE}^E$ are also rigorously defined through geometric transformations.

### II-B Problem Formulation
The goal is to simultaneously follow commanded planar velocities ($v_{d,x}^P, v_{d,y}^P$), yaw rate ($\omega_{d,z}^P$), pelvis height, and dual-arm target poses $g_{RD}$ without losing balance.
Because the robot's actuators are driven by low-level PD controllers, the overall output must be joint-position setpoints. The architecture converts task-space feedback into nominal arm joint positions, onto which the RL policy adds a residual correction. When the learned residual is zero, the nominal model-based controller's behavior is preserved.
Furthermore, if the reference frame $R$ moves, the world-frame target $g_{WD} = g_{WR} \cdot g_{RD}$ oscillates even if $g_{RD}$ is constant. It is therefore crucial to select a reference frame that retains the planar motion needed for locomotion while filtering out pelvis pitch, roll, and heave.

sections.heading: ResGAC architecture: Merging geometric control and residual RL
sections.summary: ResGAC employs a two-tier structure: floating-base geometric admittance control (GAC) generates nominal arm setpoints, while residual RL compensates for unmodeled dynamics and handles lower-body locomotion. It also details the ground-attached heading frame and the curriculum learning strategy with bilateral symmetry regularization.
sections.details:
### III-A Floating-Base Geometric Admittance Control (GAC)
First, the controller computes the relative Jacobian and relative velocity of the end-effector with respect to the moving reference frame $R$. Because simulators and real-world libraries (such as Pinocchio) typically compute Jacobians in the world frame, relative quantities are formed via an intermediate world-aligned Cartesian frame, yielding the relative body Jacobian $J_{RE}^E$.
Geometric admittance control (GAC) is then applied. While GAC is traditionally used for compliant contact control, here it functions as a geometric task-space pose tracker without force sensing, operating much like differential inverse kinematics (IK). Based on desired error dynamics, it computes a desired body twist $V_D$ and maps it through a damped pseudoinverse and nullspace projection to nominal arm joint targets $a_{\mathrm{GAC},t}$. Because this feedback law is left-invariant, the exact same control law works across different manipulation reference frames.

### III-B Residual Reinforcement Learning
To the nominal arm targets $a_{\mathrm{GAC},t}$, the RL policy adds a bounded, scaled, and clipped residual $a_{\mathrm{RL,arm},t}$. Lower-body and waist joints are commanded directly by the policy. The policy's observation vector includes the nominal GAC targets, $SE(3)$ pose errors, relative velocities, and gait phase variables. Training uses an Asymmetric Actor-Critic framework where the critic receives privileged information such as linear pelvis velocity.

### III-C Manipulation Reference Frame Selection
To prevent pelvis oscillations from propagating to the hand, three frames are compared. The pelvis frame $P$ passes all oscillations through. The heading frame $H$ isolates yaw while discarding roll and pitch. The proposed "ground-attached heading frame $H_0$" further discards vertical heave, preserving only planar $(x, y, \psi)$ motion. This geometrically decouples walking-induced vertical oscillations from the end-effector command.

### III-D Training Curriculum and Symmetry Regularization
Training proceeds through a 6-stage progressive curriculum, starting with standing at fixed targets and advancing to trajectory tracking, walking, and wide-range task-space commands. In addition, bilateral geometric symmetry (sagittal reflection) is leveraged through data augmentation and equivariance/invariance regularization in the actor and critic, greatly boosting sample efficiency and walking stability.

sections.heading: Real-world Unitree G1 validation: Millimeter tracking and challenging tasks
sections.summary: Four experiments on a real Unitree G1 humanoid evaluated standing SE(3) tracking, end-effector stabilization during walking, a 10 mm clearance peg-in-hole task, and a mime task keeping the hand fixed in space during lower-body motion. ResGAC significantly outperformed baselines such as SONIC and End-to-End RL in all evaluations.
sections.details:
### IV-A Implementation Details
Policies were trained in Isaac Sim using the Holosoma framework and FastSAC on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU across 4,096 parallel environments in roughly 16 hours. Both GAC and the policy operate at 50 Hz. On the physical robot, Pinocchio computes kinematics, and pelvis angular velocity is read from an onboard IMU.

### IV-B Standing Manipulator Tracking Performance
ResGAC was compared against baselines including E2E-RL, Decoupled-RL (GAC alone for the arm), and SONIC across four unseen arm trajectories: sweeping, step response, figure-8 ($\infty$), and pick-and-place.
ResGAC achieved the lowest translation and rotation errors across all trajectories. In the step-response and pick-and-place tests, it achieved 6.5 mm – 6.6 mm translational error and 1.37° – 1.67° rotational error, cutting translation error by 54%–67% and rotation error by ~72% compared to the best baseline. Ablation showed that pure RL without GAC (E2E-RL) lacked geometric precision, while decoupled GAC without residual corrections failed against gravity and dynamic coupling, proving both components are necessary.

### IV-C End-Effector Stabilization via Reference Frame Design
In a walking experiment requiring the robot to hold its hand steady, the pelvis frame $P$ was compared to the ground-attached heading frame $H_0$. Along the vertical ($z$) axis, the pelvis-to-hand motion propagation ratio $\rho_z$ dropped from 1.068 in $P$ to 0.884 in $H_0$, and world-frame end-effector MAE was nearly halved from 22.5 mm down to 12.6 mm, confirming that $H_0$ effectively decouples vertical stepping motions.

### IV-D Peg-in-Hole Task
The robot inserted a 25 mm diameter peg into a 35 mm diameter hole (10 mm clearance) over 20 trials. Despite OptiTrack external calibration errors, SONIC-Teleop-v1.1 achieved only a 50% success rate (10/20), whereas ResGAC attained 90% (18/20).

### IV-E World-Frame Tracking (Mime Task)
In the "Mime-man" demonstration, the robot walked forward, backward, and turned while attempting to keep its end-effector stationary in the world frame. E2E-RL drifted with 30.0 mm position and 13.75° orientation errors, whereas ResGAC maintained 8.8 mm and 2.69° errors, giving the visual impression that the hand was locked in mid-air while the body moved underneath.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what's next
sections.summary: ResGAC successfully combines geometric admittance control with residual RL to achieve high-precision SE(3) end-effector tracking during whole-body humanoid motion. Together with reference frame designs that eliminate pelvis oscillations, it provides a solid foundation for practical humanoid loco-manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented ResGAC, a whole-body control framework enabling high-precision end-effector tracking on humanoid robots.
The key to its success lies in combining geometrically sound task-space feedback from GAC with the adaptability of residual RL—handling real-world uncertainties, balance, and locomotion in a shared joint-position action space. Furthermore, adopting a left-invariant ground-attached heading frame structurally prevents pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from perturbing hand targets during walking.
Extensive real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrated sub-centimeter and degree-level standing tracking, high peg-in-hole success rates, and stable hand holding while walking, offering a promising step toward advanced mobile manipulation.

takeaways: Rather than relying purely on RL or purely on classical control, a hybrid approach combining a geometric task-space feedback backbone (GAC) with residual RL to absorb gravity and dynamic coupling is remarkably effective.

Reference frame selection is critical in humanoid manipulation: using a ground-attached heading frame ($H_0$) that strips away not just pelvis roll and pitch but also vertical heave significantly reduces hand disturbance during walking.

Operating nominal control and residual policy within a shared joint-position action space creates a practical framework: zero residual preserves safe nominal behavior, while bounded corrections yield millimeter-level accuracy.
limitations: Linear pelvis velocity cannot be directly measured with high precision from an IMU during real-world deployment, requiring linear velocity terms to be omitted from actor-side relative velocity calculations and preventing full dynamic compensation.
Walking-induced pitch oscillations act across a long arm lever arm, transmitting foot-strike shocks that geometric frame selection alone cannot fully damp out.
The real-world experiments focus on kinematic tracking and did not evaluate heavy contact-force tasks (such as forceful pushing against surfaces).
